extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of empiricist philosophy (general educated readers interested in theory of mind)
extracted.subtask_description: Clear conceptual definitions and distinctions in empiricist philosophy of mind: how simple ideas arise, varieties of modes (motion, sound, colour, taste), modes of thinking, the passions (love, hatred, desire, etc.), and the ideas of power, liberty, and volition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of simple ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: All our simple ideas come to our minds only by sensation and reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mind receives simple ideas via the senses and by reflecting on its own operations; from these it repeats and compounds ideas to form more complex ideas (including ideas extending to infinity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Other simple modes (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple modes are modifications or composed variations of simple ideas of sensation; many distinct modes can be formed though not all are named.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include modes of motion, sound, colour, taste, unity, duration, motion, power, and thinking; the mind can repeat and compound simple ideas to create many complex ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple modes of motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Words for actions like slide, roll, walk, dance, leap, etc., denote distinct simple modes—modifications of motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modes of motion correspond to modes of extension; ideas like 'swift' and 'slow' are complex ideas that combine time, space, and motion (measures made of distances of time and space).

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of sound
rubrics_metrics.description: Every articulate word and diverse notes and lengths are different modifications of sound and provide distinct ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From hearing, the mind can form almost infinite distinct ideas (e.g., tunes are complex ideas of notes of different lengths); a musician can recall a tune by reflecting on these silent ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of colour
rubrics_metrics.description: Colours present many varieties (degrees/shades), but colour modes often combine with figure to form mixed modes (e.g., beauty, rainbow).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because assemblages of colours usually include figure (as in painting or weaving), many notable colour modes are mixed modes rather than purely chromatic ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of taste and smell
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounded tastes and smells are modes made from simple ideas of taste and smell, but many have no conventional names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such modes are often left to the reader's experience because they are hard to describe in writing; lack of naming does not imply lack of distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some simple modes have no names
rubrics_metrics.description: Many simple modes that differ only slightly are ordinarily unnamed and not treated as distinct species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either people lack fine measures to distinguish them, or naming them would not be generally useful; degree-based differences (e.g., slight shades) often go unnamed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming driven by linguistic utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex ideas are given names mainly when they are practically necessary for human communication about actions and trades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terms arise where they speed communication about regularly encountered operations (e.g., specialized trade terms like 'cohobation' for chemists); ideas not commonly practiced remain unnamed among general speakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of thinking: taxonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Thinking consists of various modifications—sensation, remembrance, recollection, contemplation, reverie, attention, intention/study, dreaming, and possibly ecstasy—each yielding distinct ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sensation is the actual entrance of an idea via the senses; remembrance is recurrence without present external cause; recollection requires effort; contemplation is prolonged attention; reverie is ideas floating without reflection; attention is registering in memory; intention/study is earnest, chosen fixation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degrees and varieties of attention
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind exhibits several degrees of attention when thinking: intense study that excludes other impressions, bare observation of trains of ideas, and near indifference where ideas pass unregarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: concentrated thought can shut out sensory impressions (e.g., sleeping through thunder); mid-level attention merely notes ideas' succession; low attention treats them as faint shadows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thinking as action not essence
rubrics_metrics.description: Because thinking admits of intention and remission (degrees and variability), it is more plausibly an action of the soul than its immutable essence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The argument: operations of agents vary (admit degrees), whereas essences do not; thus the variability of thinking suggests it is an action rather than an essence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure and pain as simple ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure and pain are simple ideas received from sensation and reflection; they cannot be fully described but are known by experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defining them by 'presence of good or evil' is merely to point back to personal experience; both bodily and mental pleasures/pains count as the same kinds of simple ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good and evil defined by pleasure/pain
rubrics_metrics.description: Things are good or evil only in reference to the pleasure or pain they are apt to cause or remove.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GOOD increases pleasure or reduces pain or secures other goods; EVIL increases pain or diminishes pleasure or brings other evils. Pleasure/pain here covers both bodily and mental states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passions arise from considerations of good and evil
rubrics_metrics.description: Passions are dispositions of the mind produced by thoughts about things that cause pleasure or pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observing how things operate upon us (pleasure/pain) allows us to form ideas of passions (love, hatred, desire, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Love
rubrics_metrics.description: Love is the idea arising from reflecting on the delight a present or absent thing produces in us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: saying 'I love grapes' means the taste delights; changes in health that remove that delight remove the love.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hatred
rubrics_metrics.description: Hatred is the idea arising from reflecting on the pain a present or absent thing produces in us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hatred of inanimate things often stems from their harmful use; hatred of beings capable of happiness can come from uneasiness caused by their existence or welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desire
rubrics_metrics.description: Desire is the uneasiness felt in the absence of something whose possession would bring delight; its intensity depends on the degree of uneasiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Desire is the chief spur to action: if absence carries no uneasiness, there is mere velleity (weak wish) and no vigorous pursuit; belief in impossibility diminishes desire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joy
rubrics_metrics.description: Joy is the delight from considering present or assured near possession of a good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One can have joy anticipatorily (e.g., relief arriving to a starving person); possession in the sense of having a good readily usable also produces joy upon reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sorrow
rubrics_metrics.description: Sorrow is uneasiness arising from the thought of a lost good or the perception of present evil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts with joy; sorrow is tied to perceived loss or present suffering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hope
rubrics_metrics.description: Hope is the pleasure taken in the thought of probable future enjoyment of a desired good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hope depends on the probability or expectation of obtaining the good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fear
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear is uneasiness of mind about a likely future evil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parallels hope but oriented toward anticipated pain or harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Despair
rubrics_metrics.description: Despair is the thought of the unattainableness of any good, producing uneasiness, pain, or sometimes rest/indolency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different minds react differently: despair can cause acute pain or a resigned indifference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anger
rubrics_metrics.description: Anger is uneasiness or discomposure of the mind upon receiving an injury, accompanied by a present purpose of revenge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition links emotional state to reactive intention (revenge).

rubrics_metrics.name: Envy
rubrics_metrics.description: Envy is uneasiness caused by noticing a desired good obtained by another who we think ought not to have it before us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike simple pleasure/pain-based passions, envy and anger involve mixed considerations about ourselves and others and may not be present in all people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality of certain passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Passions terminating purely in pleasure/pain (love, desire, joy, hope, hatred, fear, grief) are likely to be found in all men; anger and envy, which involve other considerations, may not be universal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pain produces more consistent responses than pleasure, explaining asymmetry in constant affection/repayment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure/pain polarity (loss and removal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Removal or lessening of pain is experienced as pleasure; loss or diminution of pleasure is experienced as pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows interconvertibility of these states in relation to change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shame
rubrics_metrics.description: Shame is uneasiness of the mind about having done something indecent or that will lower others' esteem; its bodily signs (blushing) are not essential to the idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passions often have bodily operations, but these are not necessary parts of the mental idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idea of power: origin
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea of power arises from observing day-to-day alterations and concluding that like changes will be made in future by like agents in like ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: We consider in things both the possibility of having their simple ideas changed and the possibility of producing that change (e.g., fire has power to melt gold).

rubrics_metrics.name: Active and passive power
rubrics_metrics.description: Power is twofold: active (ability to make change) and passive (ability to receive change).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example discussion: bodies often present passive power clearly; active power (the power to begin actions) is less clearly observed in bodies and more evident by reflection on our minds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power includes relation
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea of power inherently involves relation (relation to action or change) much like other ideas include relations among parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sensible qualities (colours, smells) are in effect powers of bodies relative to our perception; ideas like extension, duration, number also connote relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearest idea of active power from spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflection on mental operations (thinking and volition) gives a clearer idea of active power than observation of bodies, which often only transfer motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bodies show transfer/continuation of motion rather than production of motion; willing shows the beginning of motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Will and understanding as two powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind contains two powers: the WILL (power to begin/forbear or order actions and motions) and the UNDERSTANDING (power of perception).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Will's exercise is volition or willing; forbearance of action is voluntary; actions done without such thought are involuntary. Understanding comprises perception of ideas, signification of signs, and relations among ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculties are not separate beings
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms like 'understanding' and 'will' (faculties) should not be reified into distinct beings in the soul—such language can mislead into imagining separate agents with provinces and authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'faculty' carefully to avoid confusion; attend to evidence and clear thinking rather than the sound of words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of ideas of liberty and necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas of LIBERTY and NECESSITY arise from reflecting on the extent of the mind's power over actions (ability to do or forbear).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal sense of power to begin/forbear actions informs whether one judges an agent free or under necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty defined (agent-level)
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberty is the power in an agent to do or forbear a particular action according to the determination of the mind; it is an attribute of the agent, not of the will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where an agent cannot equally produce or forbear an action when the mind prefers one over the other, that agent is not free. Liberty requires the power to effect the preference (examples: tennis ball has no liberty; a man locked in a room can voluntarily prefer to stay but lacks liberty to leave).

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary vs involuntary (and relation to necessity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Voluntary is opposed to involuntary; voluntary actions are those accompanied by thought/choice (even if not free), whereas involuntary lack such choice. Necessity concerns lack of power to follow volition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A man may will something he cannot perform (necessity), yet his preference or stay may still be voluntary. Examples: convulsive motions (involuntary), sitting still by a paralytic (voluntary even if limited by necessity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Volition (act of willing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Volition is the actual exercise of the will—ordering, directing, choosing, preferring—which is best grasped by reflecting on one's own acts of willing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Words like 'ordering' or 'preferring' approximate volition but require introspective reflection to understand the precise mental act; the text warns about the difficulty of capturing internal actions in language.
